_note: Where MyThuso works, and what a map of it is allowed to draw. The dispatch board used to hold its own list of suburbs, its own coordinates and its own map window inside a React component, which meant iOS and Android each invented their own Johannesburg and none of the three agreed. This file is the one Johannesburg. Read by the web app; generated into Swift and Kotlin by scripts/emit-geography.mjs. No arithmetic lives here — distance, projection, province lookup and arrival estimates are packages/geo, and a coordinate outside South Africa is refused there before it reaches a map. The tile source lives here too — the endpoint, the licence, the attribution and the usage policy — so that changing map provider is a data change and the attribution can never drift from the source it credits. Nothing in this file contacts a tile server: the web asks for streets only when the person looking has asked for them, and no native build asks at all.

coverage.sentence: Phase one is northern Johannesburg and Soweto. Everywhere else on this map is drawn because it is there, not because anybody is working in it.
coverage.whyOneCity: The funding proposal commits to a single metro first. A map that shades in the whole of Gauteng because the tiles reach that far is a map making a promise the business has not made.

window._maxZoomNote: Fifteen, deliberately. At sixteen and above a reader can pick out an individual house, and no screen in this product has a reason to. The limit is the privacy control, not a performance one.

precision.sentence: Every position in this preview is rounded to three decimal places — about a hundred metres. The suburbs are real; nobody lives at these points.
precision.why: A preview has no business being precise about where a person is standing. Three decimals is enough to draw a suburb and not enough to find a door.

rendering.whyEngine: MapLibre is the community fork of mapbox-gl: the same API, the same size, and no account. Mapbox needs a pk. token, and a token is procurement — a billing relationship, a key that can be revoked and a vendor whose expiry turns a dispatch board into a grey rectangle. The swap changed the dependency count by nothing and took one blocker off a product that has eleven others.
rendering.offSwitchNote: Set VITE_MAP_TILES=off to build without any tile source at all. The switch then does not appear and the schematic is the whole map — the state every native build is already in.

source.name: OpenFreeMap
source.licence: Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors, under the Open Database Licence. Tile schema by OpenMapTiles. The OpenFreeMap software is MIT.
source.attributionNote: This is the wording OpenFreeMap asks for, and the OpenStreetMap credit inside it is a condition of the ODbL rather than a courtesy — the licence asks that a reader can reach it, which is what attributionUrl is for. It is never suppressed, never moved off-screen and never made smaller than the type scale's floor. It is rendered from this file rather than from whatever the provider's own tile metadata happens to say: a credit supplied by the party being credited can stop being supplied without anybody noticing, and this one cannot.
source.usagePolicy: No registration, no API key and no cookies. No limit on the number of map views or requests, and commercial use is allowed — both stated in as many words. There is also no service level: the maintainer says he offers no SLA guarantees or personalised support, and the public instance is funded by donations.
source.styleWhy: Positron is the palest of the four styles offered, and this map has its own things to say. Pins, zones and the straight line are the only saturated marks on the board; a street map that competes with them is a street map that has buried the visit waiting fifty minutes.
source.whyPreviewOnly: A design preview may sit on a free public instance and this one does. A dispatch board a nurse depends on may not: there is no uptime commitment to point at, no operator agreement under POPIA, and no say in where the requests are logged or for how long. Before launch this endpoint is replaced by one MyThuso runs itself, from the planet extracts OpenFreeMap publishes weekly for exactly that purpose. Changing it is an edit to this file.
source.loadTimeoutWhy: A captive portal does not refuse a request, it answers it with a sign-in page, and a map waiting on that waits for ever. Eight seconds and the schematic comes back.

tiles.whyOff: The default is the setting nobody chooses, so it has to be the one that asks nothing of anybody. A patient opening this screen is watching for a nurse, not deciding about a mapping vendor, and on-by-default would have made the request before she had read the sentence describing it. Off also keeps the map library out of her handset until she asks for it, which on a prepaid bundle is the difference between a screen and a screen plus 1.8 MB.
tiles.offSentence: Streets are off, so the map is drawn from the coordinates alone and nothing has been asked of anybody. Turning them on asks OpenFreeMap for the streets underneath: it would then see which square of the city is on screen, the internet address that asked, and when. It is never told what is drawn on top.
tiles.onSentence: Streets are on, so OpenFreeMap has been asked for this part of the city. It can see the square on screen, the internet address that asked and the time — never the visit, never the patient and never the nurse. The closest zoom this map allows makes that square about 1.1 km across: a suburb, not a house.
tiles.notRemembered: This choice is not remembered. Streets are off again the next time this screen opens.
tiles._squareMetresNote: The width of one tile at the map's maximum zoom, at the latitude of the window centre: 40075017 × cos(lat) ÷ 2^maxZoom metres. It is the finest thing a tile request can distinguish, which is what makes 'a suburb, not a house' a measurement rather than a reassurance. tests/map.spec.ts recomputes it from window.maxZoom and fails if the sentence above and this number stop agreeing.

withoutTiles.name: Schematic
withoutTiles.sentence: This map is drawn from the coordinates alone: the zones, the visits and the nurses, in their real positions, without streets behind them. No tile server is asked for anything.
withoutTiles.why: A map that fails to a grey rectangle when a key is missing teaches a dispatcher to distrust the screen. The schematic is a complete answer to the same question — who is where — drawn from the same numbers, and it needs no network at all.

unreachable.sentence: The streets did not arrive, so the map has gone back to drawing from the coordinates alone. It answers the same question and needs no network.
unreachable.why: A tile server can be down, over its limit, or quietly replaced by the sign-in page of a clinic's wifi. All three end here rather than at a grey rectangle, because a controller who has seen one grey rectangle stops believing the board at the moment they most need to.

rendering.whySuppressed: A dispatch board is not a street directory. Positron names no shops or filling stations to begin with, so what goes is the rest of the noise: the name of the country and the province a controller is already standing in, American route shields, airports and footpath names. Suburb names, roads and water stay.
rendering.attributionNote: Attribution is a licence condition, not a design choice. The words are source.attribution and they are rendered on the map itself whenever streets are drawn.

marks.name: Service zone
marks.detail: A suburb MyThuso covers, drawn at its working radius.

marks.name: Nurse available
marks.detail: Cleared by vetting and not on a visit.

marks.name: Nurse on a visit
marks.detail: Positioned, but not dispatchable until the visit closes.

marks.name: Blocked by vetting
marks.detail: Drawn where they are and refused all the same. A lapsed credential withdraws dispatch by arithmetic, not by somebody remembering.

marks.name: Visit awaiting a nurse
marks.detail: Plotted at the centre of its suburb, never at its address.

privacy.sentence: A map in MyThuso plots suburbs, not addresses.

rules.statement: A visit awaiting a nurse is drawn at the centre of its suburb. Its street address is never a coordinate on any map, on any screen, at any zoom.
rules.why: A home address beside a health service is not a location, it is a diagnosis with a doorstep. The controller assigning the visit needs to know which suburb it is in; they do not need to know which house until they are the one going to it, and then it is in the visit, not on the board.

rules.statement: A nurse who is not sharing a position has none, and the board says so rather than placing them somewhere plausible.
rules.why: An empty space is a true statement about a phone in a bag. A guessed pin is a false statement about a person's whereabouts, and it is the one a dispatcher would act on.

rules.statement: No map here draws where anybody has been. A position is the current one or it is absent.
rules.why: A track is a record of a person's movements. Nothing in this product needs one, so nothing in this product keeps one, and there is no screen that could be persuaded to show one.

rules.statement: MyThuso shows you where a nurse is on the day of your visit and not before. A nurse’s whereabouts between visits is her own, in the same way your address is yours.
rules.why: The sharpest rule on the patient's half of this map, and it is arithmetic rather than copy: no state that draws a nurse is reachable unless the visit is today, so there is no path through arrival that puts her on a map a fortnight early. A patient who can open a screen a fortnight before her appointment and watch a nurse move around Johannesburg has been handed a tracking device, and no part of arranging a home visit needs one. Before the day there is nothing to watch, and the screen says so rather than drawing an empty map.

rules.statement: A nurse is drawn in the suburb she is working in, and your visit is drawn in the centre of yours — at both ends, at every zoom.
rules.why: address-is-not-a-pin read the other way round. That rule protects the patient's door from the board; this one protects the nurse's position from the patient, and says so in the same breath so neither reads as the exception. A nurse's working day is her private life as much as an address is somebody's.

rules.statement: Nothing on this screen is being measured. No nurse’s device is read, no arrival is timed against your window, and nobody has been told you are watching.
rules.why: A patient looking at a moving estimate assumes somebody is watching back. Nobody is: the positions are this file's own zone centres, no geolocation permission is requested by any platform, and opening the screen is not an event anybody is sent. Said out loud on the screen, because the assumption is the thing that needs correcting.

rules.statement: The tile server is asked for streets. It is never told what is on top of them — no visit, no patient, no nurse position is sent to any mapping provider.
rules.why: A map vendor that can see your pins can see your caseload. The zones, the visits and the nurses are drawn by this application on top of tiles that know nothing about them.

rules.statement: Asking for streets still tells the tile server something: which square of the map is open, the internet address that asked, and the time. Over a visit that is roughly which suburb a patient is in and roughly when somebody came to the house. Streets are off until the person looking turns them on, and the schematic asks nobody anything.
rules.why: Until this map drew streets no tile was ever fetched, so there was nothing to disclose and nobody had disclosed it. Now there is. A viewport is not a pin, but a health service whose viewports a third party can watch has handed over a weaker version of the same thing, and one nobody agreed to. The sentence is rendered beside the switch rather than filed in a policy page, because the switch is where the decision is actually made.

refusals.sentence: Nobody is on the way yet, so there is nothing to follow. You will see where she is on the day of your visit.
refusals.why: What a patient reads ahead of the day. It says what is refused and leaves her somewhere to stand, which is the difference between a state and a blank — and it does not repeat the rule underneath it, because only-on-the-day is said once in the list of what this screen is not.

refusals.sentence: This visit has no time yet, so there is nobody assigned to be on the way. When a nurse accepts it you will be told who is coming and when.
refusals.why: An as-soon-as-possible visit has no window, and a visit with no window has not been accepted by anybody. Drawing a nurse for it would invent an assignment that has not happened.

refusals.sentence: This visit is not ahead of you, so there is nothing to follow. What happened at it is in the visit itself.
refusals.why: A past or cancelled visit has no arrival. The screen sends the reader to the record rather than to an empty map, because the question behind opening it is usually about what was found.

refusals.sentence: This is not an arrival time. It is the distance between two suburbs, divided by a speed — it does not know the traffic, the road, or the visit she is finishing first.
refusals.why: No routing provider is connected, and a straight line through Johannesburg is optimistic by roughly a third. The figure is shown because a patient waiting at home is owed something; the sentence carrying it refuses the promise the figure looks like, in the same breath, rather than in a footnote.

refusals.sentence: That position is not in South Africa. It has not been drawn.
refusals.why: packages/geo refuses the coordinate before a map sees it. A pin in the Atlantic is a data fault, and the map's job is to be the place it becomes visible rather than the place it is smoothed over.

refusals.sentence: MyThuso is not working in that area yet. You can be told when it is.
refusals.why: Refusing a booking outside phase one is the whole point of naming a phase. An app that takes the booking anyway has moved the disappointment to the patient's front door.

refusals.sentence: This nurse is not sharing a position right now, so they are not on the map.
refusals.why: Said out loud, on the board, next to the count. A dispatcher who cannot see the difference between nobody-there and nobody-reporting will read the map as the first one.
